CHIEF COMPLAINT
Back of the heel hurts typically after a workout or when first getting up in the morning, all the way up into the calf.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is training for a triathlon (running about 10 kilometers in the morning, biking 45 minutes to an hour at lunchtime, and swimming 30 minutes to an hour in the evening, 5 days a week; on weekends alternates between a long run and a long bike ride, taking 1 day off). He does not stretch at all. He presents with pain in the back of his right heel and calf that occurs after activity and is also present when first waking up in the morning, feeling very tight and almost like it's tearing. It eases up a little after walking around for 10-15 minutes, but becomes really sore again after sitting for an extended period or after a lot of activity. Pain is mainly on the right side.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities examined. Right leg shows pain when pulling toes up towards him, and when pushing against the doctor's hand. Patient rolled over onto stretcher and dangled feet; left calf squeeze caused no pain on the left side. Right calf squeeze showed no pain there. Thompson test is negative. Pressing on the right heel causes significant pain, and running up the Achilles tendon is described as really tender.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Diagnosis: Achilles tendinitis, from overuse related to aggressive triathlon training.
Plan:
- Stop training for a week or two to allow healing.
- Take ibuprofen or Advil, three tablets every six hours as an anti-inflammatory.
- Order a couple of physical therapy visits to gain strength and stretching understanding, and learn how to stretch muscles before activities.
- Follow up in 7 to 10 days following the first couple of physical therapy appointments to monitor progress.
- No x-ray indicated at this time, but more aggressive treatment plans may be considered if significant pain continues after 10 days without activity modification.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems (depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history of depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair, presenting for a routine follow-up. He reports doing well overall over the past six months. For his depression, he sees a counselor once a week and goes swimming frequently; he does not wish to start medications at this time. For his hypertension, he takes Norvasc daily and checks his blood pressure at CVS once a week, noting occasional dietary indiscretions with burgers and wine. He reports mild ankle swelling near the end of the day that resolves by the next morning. For his rotator cuff repair from about 8 months ago, he is doing well, stretching with a yoga ball, progressing to home exercises, and gaining strength.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Positive for mild ankle swelling near the end of the day that resolves by morning. Review of systems otherwise unremarkable per the check-in sheet.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vital signs: Blood pressure elevated at 156/94.
- Heart: 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, stable compared to the past.
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
- Lower extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema in the legs.

RESULTS
- Labs: Creatinine and kidney function look stable; overall lab results look really good. (Note: Lipid panel ordered).
- EKG: Normal EKG, fine, with no evidence of coronary artery disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well with counseling and swimming. No medication indicated at this time; patient knows to call if needed.
2. Hypertension: Not well controlled. Increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily. Order an echocardiogram and a lipid panel. Discussed decreasing salt intake to help with lower extremity edema.
3. Rotator cuff repair: Doing very well with home exercises and yoga ball stretching. Considered resolved; no further intervention needed.

Follow-up visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female here for follow-up. Her diabetes is not well controlled, with a recent A1c of 9.9. She is currently taking glimepiride 2 mg, and the plan is to increase it to 4 mg twice a day (taking two of her current 2 mg pills twice a day, with a new prescription for 4 mg twice a day). She also continues metformin. She tries to eat healthy, avoids pasta, rarely eats bread (uses wheat bread when she does), drinks club soda and seltzer water, and does not drink regular water or sodas. She had cataract surgery recently and got new glasses, seeing Dr. Sanchez at Liberty Road. She has a history of high blood pressure and takes metoprolol 50 mg once a day, lisinopril with hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg once a day, and amlodipine 10 mg once a day. She reports her feet "feel like hell" and her legs bug her all the time, limiting her walking; she notes pain up to her hip. She admits she is still smoking and is not ready to quit. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Feeling totally normal. No headaches, dizziness, fever, or chills.
HEENT: Vision is better with cataract surgery, though she is not entirely happy with one lens.
Respiratory: Coughing lately due to congestion with relatively clear mucus. No shortness of breath or wheezing.
Cardiovascular: No chest pains, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or other GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Slower stream but stable, urinates several times per day, gets up at night once in a while.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in hips and upper legs, difficulty walking attributed to peripheral neuropathy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Carotids: Normal, pulse without bruits.
Heart: Rhythm is regular, normal rate, S1 and S2 are crisp, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear, no rasps or wheezing.
Extremities: Without edema. Pulses palpable on dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin, no skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetes mellitus: A1c was 9.9. Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day (take two 2 mg pills twice a day of current supply; new prescription for 4 mg twice a day). Continue metformin. Watch for signs of low blood sugar (weak, shaky, sweaty).

4. Hyperlipidemia / Vascular disease: Continue atorvastatin.
5. Tobacco use: Patient continues to smoke; counseling provided.
6. Labs: Blood work to be drawn today, including kidney function and blood work.
7. Follow-up: Return in four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up from emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure who presents for follow-up after an ER visit. On Saturday, while playing tennis in hot and humid weather, he experienced shortness of breath and difficulty breathing after about half an hour. He thought he was having a heart attack, got nervous, and his wife took him to the ER. Everything checked out at the ER, but he was very upset about it. About six hours after getting home, he felt very lightheaded and dizzy, but felt fine by Sunday. He has been taking all his heart failure medications diligently and watching his diet, though he admits to occasional dietary indiscretions with salty foods. He also reports that his cataract surgery from three months ago and skin cancer removal from five months ago have both healed nicely with no ongoing problems.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: No acute distress. 
Eyes: No vision problems.
Cardiovascular: History of congestive heart failure; experienced shortness of breath, lightheadedness, and dizziness following tennis in the heat. 
Respiratory: Shortness of breath on Saturday.
Skin: Skin cancer removed 5 months ago, healed nicely with no current issues.
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Supple, no jugular venous distention appreciated.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur.
Lungs: Fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema in both legs.
Vitals: Blood pressure is a little high (noted to be high in the ER as well).

RESULTS
ECG: Stable ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low, but stable.
Skin Biopsy Pathology Report: Margins clear, all skin cancer was removed, everything is fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath / Congestive heart failure exacerbation: Likely precipitated by heat and dietary indiscretion (salty foods) leading to fluid retention. 
- Prescribe an extra dose of Lasix 80 mg once a day.
- Start Carvedilol 25 mg twice a day.
2. Blood pressure: Elevated; will monitor.
3. Status-post cataract surgery and skin cancer removal: Doing well, no medication adjustments needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a male presenting with lower back pain that began approximately four months ago while moving boxes during his son's college move-out. Initially, he experienced a brief sensation of feeling like he was going to topple over and inability to support his upper body weight, along with tingling in the toes of his right foot that resolved after about an hour. He reports occasional sharp pain in the lower back when turning a certain way or rolling over in sleep, which resolves with repositioning. He feels weak in the legs only when carrying heavy items. He tried Tylenol, ibuprofen (which provides short-term relief), heat, and ice without significant relief, as well as some physical therapy at his gym which did not help. He went to urgent care previously where an MRI was recommended, but he did not complete it due to insurance cost concerns. He denies bladder or bowel incontinence or retention, and denies fevers or chills.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Negative for fevers or chills.
Neurological: Brief initial right toe tingling (resolved); no current numbness or tingling.
Musculoskeletal: Lower back pain, stiffness, and weakness when carrying heavy items. No bowel or bladder changes.
All other systems reviewed and negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 117/56, heart rate 68, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, afebrile.
Neck: Bony protuberance of C5-C6 noted; no pain to palpation.
Lumbar Spine: No pain to palpation of the lumbar spine. Decreased flexion and extension of the lower back. Positive straight leg raise. Spasm of the paraspinal muscles of the lumbar spine.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength is equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine x-ray showed no acute bony abnormality and no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute disc herniation (suspected, based on ongoing symptoms).
2. Order lumbar spine MRI to evaluate soft tissues.
3. Continue physical therapy; refer to a physical therapist through the health system.
4. Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg once a day.
5. Discussed potential future treatment options if herniated disc is confirmed, such as an epidural steroid injection.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on it.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elijah is a patient referred by his primary care provider who presents with right foot pain after dropping a landscape brick on his foot yesterday while doing yard work. He was able to keep working initially despite the pain, but the foot subsequently became swollen. He rates his pain as an 11 out of 10. He reports numbness of the entire foot, which he states has been present for a long time. He has not taken any medications for the pain. He reports a past medical history of breaking his ankle 20 years ago, which occasionally causes soreness and swelling, as well as prior surgery on his other ankle.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Look good.
Right foot: Bruising on the bottom and top parts of the foot. Associated swelling present. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot.
Neurovascular: Capillary refill is brisk in less than three seconds. Strong bounding dorsalis pedis pulse. Motor and sensation are intact. Findings match bilaterally.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: Shows dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases and presence of bony fragments.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Right foot pain due to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone and the top of the foot).
- Order an MRI (facility is downstairs; to be done this afternoon) to assess for any injuries to the ligaments.
- Patient will most likely need outpatient surgery (same-day procedure involving plates and screws to align bones and ligaments properly, prevent loss of arch/flat-footedness, and reduce risk of arthritis). Surgery discussed for tomorrow, though patient stated they would like some time to think about it.
- Post-procedure plan: Cast, crutches, non-weight-bearing for 6 to 8 weeks, gradual advancement of ambulation based on healing. Follow-up in 24 hours post-procedure and again in two weeks.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Elevated and fluctuating blood pressures.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ISSUES
Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis, presenting with concerns about elevated and fluctuating blood pressures over the past 3 to 4 weeks. He reports occasional upper blood pressure readings over 180, along with periods of lightheadedness, slight headaches, and feeling a little unsteady when dizzy. He notes occasional mild heaviness in his chest, but denies sustained chest pain, respiratory difficulty, passing out recently, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or palpitations. He is currently taking lisinopril 20 mg twice daily (very rarely missing doses) and atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. For osteoarthritis, he manages mild pain with Tylenol and activity modification.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever.
HEENT: Slight headache associated with higher blood pressure numbers.
Cardiovascular: Occasional mild heaviness in chest; no sustained chest pain or palpitations.
Respiratory: No breathing difficulty or respiratory issues.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Neurological: Lightheadedness/dizziness, feeling a little fuzzy, unsteadiness with dizziness; no numbness, weakness, or balance instability other than with dizziness. No recent syncope.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pretty normal and unremarkable.
Heart: Grade 3 out of 6 systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior.
Lungs: Mild bibasilar rales; no wheezes or rhonchi; excellent air movement.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Essential Hypertension: Out of control. Increase lisinopril to 60 mg twice per day and add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg per day. Check blood pressure measurements twice a day for the next two weeks. Stay well-hydrated (6-8 glasses of water per day). Limit alcohol intake to no more than a couple of drinks a week.
2. Hyperlipidemia: Continue current management with atorvastatin. Order labs: cholesterol panel, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis to check kidney function.
3. Osteoarthritis: Continue to stay active as best as possible (walking, golfing), use Tylenol for mild pain as needed.
Follow-up: Return in two weeks to recheck blood pressure and progress.

Right-sided back pain and blood in urine.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an individual who presents with right-sided back pain for about a week, which has moved down slightly to the right lower side. The pain is described as pretty constant. She also noticed some blood in her urine, but no real pain with urination. She took ibuprofen, which helped a little bit, but it still hurts. She reports feeling a little bit nauseated, but no vomiting, fever, or chills. This is her first time experiencing a kidney stone, though her dad had kidney stones. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: No fever or chills. 
Gastrointestinal: Mild nausea; no vomiting. 
Genitourinary: Blood in urine, no dysuria. 
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Good, no fever, blood pressure and heart rate are fine.
Abdomen: Mild pain and tenderness to palpation of the abdomen. No rebound or guarding. CVA located near flank tenderness on the right.

RESULTS
CT scan of the side showed a stone measuring 0.5 centimeters in size located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right kidney stone (0.5 cm in the proximal right ureter).
2. Recommend pushing fluids to help facilitate passing the stone.
3. Prescribe ibuprofen 800 mg as needed for pain.
4. Provide a urine strainer to catch the stone when it passes.
5. Order a BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture; evaluate for possible antibiotics if a urinary infection is present.
6. Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks. If still having symptoms, discuss further treatment such as lithotripsy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right upper quadrant abdominal pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a patient referred by Dr. Miller for evaluation of belly pain present for several weeks. An outside ultrasound previously showed gallstones. The patient describes the pain as located on the right side of the belly right underneath the ribs, feeling like a severe squeezing pain that comes and goes. When severe, the pain is rated as an 8 out of 10. The pain occurs mostly right after eating or a couple of hours later. Associated symptoms include nausea, no vomiting, and occasional low-grade fevers when the pain is really bad for a couple of days. The patient has cut back on sugar and started a keto diet, losing about 25 pounds over the last three months. Cutting out fatty foods like pork rinds has helped a little bit, but the pain persists. Family history is positive for gallbladder disease in both parents, who both had their gallbladders removed. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Positive for occasional low-grade fevers when pain is severe. 
Gastrointestinal: Positive for right upper quadrant abdominal pain related to meals, nausea, and no vomiting. 
All other systems reviewed and negative in detail.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 128/88, respiratory rate 16, pulse rate 68, afebrile, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
General: Appears in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no ectopic beats, clicks, rubs, or murmurs.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Abdomen: Positive bowel sounds, soft, nondistended. Positive for slight guarding in the right upper quadrant; no rebound tenderness. Positive Murphy's sign (patient exhibited guarding and reported severe pain with palpation beneath the right ribs during inspiration). No peritoneal signs.

RESULTS
Abdominal ultrasound: Shows multiple gallstones present in the gallbladder with mild thickening. Common bile duct size is within normal limits at 4.1 millimeters.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Mild cholecystitis with gallstones, without frank obstruction.
2. Recommended laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The procedure will take about 1 to 1.5 hours, and the patient will likely spend one night in the hospital for post-procedure monitoring.
3. Post-procedure instructions: Continue to avoid high-frequency/high-fat foods and eat high-fiber foods. Take it easy for the first 24 hours, but can walk around on solid ground within a day or two. Follow-up in about one week to review for release to return to normal nature activities.
4. Advised to follow up with primary care physician or endocrinologist regarding type 2 diabetes management around the time of surgery.

Knee injury and pain.

She wears a brace, uses THC cream, and takes THC gummies given by her grandma to help with pain. She notes significant swelling and morning stiffness in the knee until she starts walking. Past medical history includes previous right knee surgery at age 14 after feeling a pop during a back somersault in gymnastics, where she was told the whole knee was reconstructed. She normally skis about three times a week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies other issues. 
Musculoskeletal: Positive for right knee pain (medial aspect), right knee swelling, morning stiffness, and instability in the left knee. Denies pain on the outside of the right knee. Pain occasionally radiates as a shooting pain down to the ankle when the kneecap is moved.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Skin: Mild swelling and bruising on the right knee, present two weeks post-injury. Range of motion: Able to bend the right knee.

She has two inhalers prescribed previously but only uses the albuterol; the other does not seem to work for her. She occasionally goes to bars where secondhand smoke irritates her breathing, so she tries to avoid going often.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left foot pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Jean is a soccer player who presents with left foot pain after an injury during a soccer game yesterday. She was trying to steal the ball from another player who fell directly onto her right foot (noting later in the exam discussion that the injury is to the left foot), and her body twisted around the player, resulting in sudden foot pain. She was unable to continue playing and had to be helped off the field. She has been treating the pain with elevation, ice, a wrap applied by the trainer yesterday, and ibuprofen. Pain level is a 3 out of 10 with ibuprofen and 7 to 8 out of 10 without ibuprofen. She denies any numbness, tingling, or strange sensations in the left foot. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies numbness, tingling, or strange sensations in the left foot. Otherwise, not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 58, respiratory rate 14, afebrile, O2 saturation 99% on room air.
General/Constitutional: Not discussed.
HEENT: Not discussed.
Neck: Not discussed.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no clicks, rubs, murmurs, or ectopic beats noted on auscultation.
Respiratory: Lungs clear and equal bilaterally, moving good air.
Gastrointestinal: Not discussed.
Musculoskeletal / Focused Foot Exam (Left Foot): Bruising on the bottom and top of the foot. Associated swelling present. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test. 
Neuromuscular / Neurovascular: Brisk capillary refill of less than three seconds, dorsalis pedis pulse intact and strong, motor and sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Diagnostic imaging (X-ray) shows subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Left foot pain secondary to a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone where metatarsals meet the cuboids).
- Order an MRI to assess for injury to ligaments at the top of the foot.
- Patient will most likely need outpatient day surgery to place bones back in proper position using plates and screws to hold them while healing.
- Patient will be in a cast, use crutches, and be non-weight-bearing on the left foot for about 6 to 8 weeks, followed by gradual return to walking based on tolerance.
- Discussed risks of not undergoing surgery, including loss of the arch of the foot (becoming flat-footed) and high likelihood of developing arthritis.
- Patient will be out for the rest of the soccer season.
- Nurse will provide paperwork, and patient will follow up with the doctor on Monday morning.

Sore on the right foot that is not healing.

The patient is a male with a history of diabetes who presents with a wound on his right foot of 2 to 3 weeks duration. He states he bought a new pair of shoes (Hokas) to travel with, and due to neuropathy, he did not feel they were too tight initially. It started as a blister and worsened. He saw his PCP, who referred him to podiatry and prescribed antibiotics; the patient finished the course yesterday, but the wound looks about the same. He reports no pain due to neuropathy. He notes that sometimes his sock sticks to the wound. He denies fever, chills, or drainage. He is no longer wearing the offending shoes. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies fever, chills.
Cardiovascular/Peripheral Vascular: Denies pain. 
All other systems not specifically discussed are negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Temperature 98.1 F, heart rate 72, respirations 16, blood pressure 110/65.
Foot Exam: 1 x 2 inch circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the 5th MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. No surrounding erythema or cellulitis, no evidence of fluid collection, no necrosis, no odor. No bony exposure appreciated. 
Vascular Exam: Palpable bilateral femoral and popliteal pulses. No palpable DP or PT pulses, but Doppler signals are present.
Neurological: Patient reports no pain to touch at the wound site.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray: Shows no evidence of osteomyelitis (no evidence of bone infection).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right foot:

- Perform in-office debridement to remove dead tissue.
- Prescribe collagenase ointment to be applied to the wound once daily, covered with a dry sterile dressing, continuing until the wound shrinks and pink tissue is present.
- Patient to wear a surgical shoe to offload pressure from the area.
- No further antibiotics needed at this time.
- Follow-up in two weeks.
- Potential referral to a vascular specialist if ABI indicates suboptimal blood supply.
2. Diabetes mellitus:
- Goal to get diabetes under control to aid wound healing.
- Consider a diabetic consult for diet modification to help lower hemoglobin A1c (last reported a little over 8).

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a female who presents with right foot pain after an injury playing tennis a couple of days ago. She states she was trying to volley the ball during a doubles game, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her foot. She twisted around to catch herself and felt pain in her foot. She was unable to continue playing and had to be held from the field because she could not put weight on her foot. Since the injury, she wrapped it with an ace wrap from the clubhouse, iced it last night, kept it elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen, which helps a little bit before wearing off. She reports no numbness or tingling and states she can still feel her foot. She has no prior history of injury to this foot, though she previously injured her other foot. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No reported fever (feels normal temperature). 
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in the right foot; sensation is intact. 
All other systems reviewed and negative except as noted in HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 125/70, respiratory rate 18, temperature 97.1 F, oxygen saturation 100%, pulse 60 bpm.
General: Appears in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops appreciated.
Respiratory: Stridor appreciated; no wheezes or rales.
Abdominal: No rebound tenderness, no guarding.
Head/Skin: Head is symmetrical, mucosal membranes are normal, not hot to touch.
Right Foot Exam: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot with associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch. Neurovascular exam shows capillary refill less than 3 seconds, strong dorsalis pedis pulse, and sensation intact to light touch.
Left Foot Exam: Normal, appropriate capillary refill, strong pedal pulses, and intact sensation.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right foot: Showed subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal with a 3-millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and the presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture (fracture to the second metatarsal bone near the top of the foot).
2. Recommend surgery to place bones in proper positions using plates and screws to prevent complications such as poor bone alignment, poor ligament healing, loss of the arch of the foot (flat-footedness), and arthritis. The procedure is a day surgery, and the patient will be able to go home the same day. 
3. Order an MRI of the right foot to further assess the fracture and any injury to the ligaments.
4. Post-procedure plan: The patient will be in a cast, use crutches, and will not be able to bear weight on the foot for 6 to 8 weeks. Will follow up in the clinic in about a week. Driving will be restricted, and she will need someone to take her home.
5. Physical therapy is recommended after surgery to strengthen muscles and ensure peak performance before returning to activity.
6. The patient is out for the rest of the tennis season.
7. Risks of surgical procedure (bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) will be reviewed with the patient via paperwork and staff.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Nonhealing foot ulcer.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a patient with type 2 diabetes who presents with a nonhealing foot ulcer on the right foot present for about a year. It started as a small blister with no trauma, which the patient picked at, became red and infected, and was treated with Keflex by the primary care physician about five months ago. The patient reports no pain due to foot neuropathy. Recently, there has been an increase in drainage and the patient feels a bit more tired. The patient denies fever or chills. Blood sugars are reported in the 200s, and the last A1c was about 10, with medications including metformin and insulin. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for feeling a little more tired. Negative for fever and chills.
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Vitals look good. No fever.
Right Foot Exam: 1 x 2 centimeter circular wound on the dorsal aspect of the lateral right foot, just proximal to the fifth MTP joint. Yellow slough present with minimal granulation tissue. No surrounding erythema or cellulitis. No evidence of fluid collection. No necrosis (dead tissue). No odor. No bony exposure. No pain to palpation (neuropathy present).

RESULTS
Right foot x-ray: Showed no evidence of osteomyelitis (no bone infection).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diabetic foot ulcer on the right foot, present for about a year.
2. Order an Ankle Brachial Index (ABI) to determine blood supply and assess healing potential.
3. Perform in-office debridement to remove tissue.
4. Prescribe collagenase ointment to be applied to the wound once a day, covered with a sterile dressing, continuing until the wound starts to shrink.
5. Provide a surgical shoe to take pressure off the area and offload the wound.
6. Advise follow-up with primary care physician regarding poorly controlled diabetes (A1c around 10, blood sugars in the 200s on metformin and insulin).
7. Return visit in two weeks for re-evaluation and possible repeat debridement.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right eye twitch.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presents for evaluation of a new right eye twitch, accompanied by her father. The father noticed the twitch a couple of weeks ago. It occurs daily, varying from several times an hour to not appearing until the late afternoon. The patient feels her face sometimes before it moves, describes an urge to move her face, and feels better afterward. The twitch involves the whole side of her face, lasts for several seconds, and ends with frequent blinking. The father notes she continues playing or doing whatever she was doing when it happens, seems fine overall, eats well, plays with friends, and goes about normal activities. There is no history of seizures. The father brought a video of the twitch to show the doctor. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for pain associated with the twitch, fever, chills, coughing, headaches, sleep problems, and family history of seizures or Tourette's syndrome. Otherwise, general review of systems is unremarkable; she has been acting normally and eating well.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological exam: Patient is awake, alert, and oriented times three. Speech is clear and fluent. Gait is steady, and heel-toe walking is normal. Cranial nerves are intact without focal neurologic findings. There is no pronator drift. Sensation is intact. Reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at the biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Facial tic / transient tics. Tics are common in children and are brief, sudden, and involuntary motor movements. Most tics go away on their own within a year. 
2. Plan: Best approach is to ignore the tics so as not to draw attention to them, which can make the child conscious of them and worsen the tic. They may wax and wane and be more noticeable when the child is tired or stressed. No treatment (pills or creams) is recommended at this time since she is doing well overall and it hasn't impacted her activities, but treatment can be considered if it worsens.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Difficulty swallowing and chest pain when swallowing.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male who presents with difficulty swallowing certain foods and pain when swallowing down in his chest for the last several weeks. Reports that bigger pieces of food seem to get stuck, but it does not happen every time he eats. Associated with recent stress due to moving from the west coast to the east coast, leading to a diet higher in fast foods like pizza and burgers, as well as increased alcohol and caffeine intake. Denies weight loss; instead, reports weight gain. Reports occasional upper belly pain (epigastric pain). Denies blood in stool or dark tarry stools, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies weight loss; notes weight gain.
Gastrointestinal: Reports difficulty swallowing, chest pain with swallowing, and occasional upper abdominal (epigastric) pain. Denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood in stool, or dark tarry stools.
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 133/70, heart rate normal, afebrile, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, respiratory rate 19. Weight noted to have increased by about 10 pounds over the last month.
HEENM: Mouth exam shows no obvious ulcers or evidence of thrush; tonsils midline. Neck shows no adenopathy and no thyromegaly. Eyes are equal and reactive to light.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. No rash, lesion, or bruising.
Abdomen: Nondistended with active bowel sounds. Pain to palpation of the epigastric area. Negative Murphy's sign. No peritoneal signs, no rebound tenderness.

RESULTS
Barium swallow showed two areas of mild narrowing in the mid and lower portions of the esophagus, consistent with esophagitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute esophagitis.
- Prescribed Protonix 40 mg once daily, to be taken first thing in the morning.
- Prescribed Carafate 1 gram four times a day for one month to coat the lining of the esophagus and stomach.
- Schedule an upper endoscopy for next week.
- Diet modification: Encourage changing diet, decreasing alcohol and caffeine, avoiding citrus fruits and spicy foods until symptoms improve, eating slowly, and chewing food more thoroughly.
- Follow-up visit scheduled for next week for the endoscopy.

Difficulty swallowing.

Tyler is a 56-year-old male with a past medical history of diabetes and high blood pressure who presents with difficulty swallowing over the last 4 to 5 weeks. He reports feeling like something is always stuck in his throat, which is occasionally a little painful. He has to wash down solid foods on occasion, though he has never fully choked. Symptoms occur primarily with solids rather than liquids, and there is no temperature-related modification with hot or cold liquids. He denies vomiting blood, coughing up blood, other bleeding, weight loss, chest pain, or shortness of breath. 

Regarding his diabetes, he takes metformin 500 mg twice a day, checks his blood sugars about 80% of the time, and reports numbers are within the targeted range. He denies nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or other side effects from metformin. Regarding his hypertension, he takes Norvasc and checks his blood pressure periodically, noting it is usually close to or on range.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for coughing, vomiting blood, coughing up blood, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. 

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Fine, no swelling, thyroid feels normal, no masses, no lymphadenopathy, no carotid bruit.
Throat: Looks okay, no masses, no swelling, no redness.
Lungs: Clear.
Heart: Normal, no murmurs.
Abdomen: Epigastric tenderness present where pressed, no masses, no significant swelling.
Back: Normal.
Extremities: Normal.
Neurological: Fine.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Difficulty swallowing: Suspect esophageal narrowing, stricture, or potential hiatal hernia. 
   - Provide a referral to gastroenterology for an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (scope).
   - Start Prilosec 20 mg once daily.

Acne on the face.

Not discussed.

Right knee pain and swelling.

He states his knee is still swollen and pretty painful, and now the whole leg is getting swollen. Current pain level is about a 3, but typically on a normal day it is around 6. The whole leg swelling has been present for about two months. He tried wearing compression socks, which help to some degree, but it is still swollen, especially around the knee. The pain keeps him from doing things during the day; he has slowed down a little bit and found a few things too fast. Pain is worst after sitting for a while, causing severe stiffness when trying to get up, requiring a cane to get his bearings until it loosens up. Not discussed.

CMP levels are good.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis with right knee pain and inflammation.
2. Right knee fluid aspiration and steroid injection performed today: Risks, benefits, and alternatives were explained, including hypopigmentation, soft tissue atrophy, tendon ruptures, and transient hypoglycemia. CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and stiffness following a motor vehicle accident.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old male presenting for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. He sustained a hyperextension injury to the right index finger during a motor vehicle accident in March of this year (approximately three months ago) when he was rear-ended and felt his finger stretch backwards. He reports ongoing swelling, inability to make a fist, and pain that is sometimes unbearable, even making driving hurt. He previously saw an orthopedist and an occupational therapist, and underwent physical therapy. An MRI was obtained on 4/24/2021. He was told he had a tear in his finger. He was initially told he would not get an injection because it might make the tear worse, and later was offered an injection, but is seeking a second opinion because he feels he is not getting proper medical care. He works as an x-ray tech and is right-handed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Takes a blood pressure medication. Reports a history of itching with methylprednisolone.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male, no distress.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulses.
Right Hand / Index Finger: No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases, slightly diminished over the PIP of the index finger compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Attempting to correct the position causes discomfort, and the patient reports a numb feeling. Bending the tip and the finger causes pain and a sensation of tearing.

RESULTS
MRI (4/24/2021): Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right FDS, and fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact, as is the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons deemed intact.
X-rays (Right hand, 4 views today): No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on the right hand, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger with a partial tear of the FDS tendon.
2. Cortisone injection attempted: Attempted to inject 1 cc of Celestone with 0.5 cc of lidocaine into the flexor tendon sheath. The patient had a dramatic and violent painful reaction on the first attempt, requiring needle withdrawal. A second attempt was performed using the same technique with 1 cc of Celestone and 0.5 cc of lidocaine. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned up and a band-aid applied.
3. Post-procedure care: Reassured the patient, recommended icing this evening, and taking ibuprofen. Driving is permitted.
4. Physical therapy / Range of motion: Outpatient physical therapy once a week for six weeks with the goal of full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lung nodule found incidentally on chest X-ray.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Kyle is a patient with a history of a cough lasting off and on for about three months, initially worsened after loading hay and following a cold. The cough has since resolved. He was evaluated by his PCP for the cough, diagnosed with bronchitis, and underwent a chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia, which incidentally revealed a lung nodule. A subsequent CT scan confirmed the finding, and he was referred to surgery. The patient is a former smoker who quit about 7 years ago. He has a history of rheumatoid arthritis managed with methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly, currently fair and with no recent flares. He denies any current pain or shortness of breath. Family history is negative for lung cancer; mother had breast cancer and is doing well. No previous history of lung infections or pneumonia.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Denies fever (afebrile).
Respiratory: Denies cough (resolved), denies shortness of breath.
Cardiovascular: Denies pain.
All other systems not specifically discussed are negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 124/76, heart rate 70, respiration rate 16, O2 saturation 98% on room air, afebrile.
Lungs: Clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm; no clicks, rubs, murmurs, or extra beats.
Extremities: Skin is pink, warm, and dry. No lower extremity edema. Mild swelling noted to knuckles on the third digit of each hand (consistent with rheumatoid arthritis). Pulses are intact in all extremities, and capillary refill is brisk.

RESULTS
Chest CT: Shows a solitary 2 cm nodule in the lateral aspect of the right upper lobe. The nodule is smooth in appearance. No evidence of emphysematous disease.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Incidentally found right upper lobe lung nodule:
- Order pulmonary function tests (PFTs) to establish a baseline for lung function.
- Schedule a PET CT scan to determine metabolic activity of the nodule.
- Recommend removal of the nodule via video-assisted thoracoscopy (VATS) utilizing three small incisions on the right chest with a camera and scope to remove the nodule and a small portion of the lung under general anesthesia.
- Anticipated procedure duration is about an hour and a half.
- Post-procedure: Admission for one night with a chest tube to be removed at bedside the following day, anticipating discharge home the next day.
- Removal is recommended due to the patient's smoking history, though the nodule could be benign.

2. Rheumatoid arthritis:
- Continue to follow up with rheumatologist and maintain current medication therapy (methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly).

Michelle King is a 39-year-old female referred by Dr. Scott for evaluation of poorly controlled acid reflux. She has had acid reflux since around age 12, which has worsened over the past few years. She currently takes omeprazole 40 mg twice daily, which she has been on for about a year. While some days are fine, others involve burning in her chest and throat, particularly triggered by stress, spicy foods, sodas/carbonation, citrus, and tomato-based products. She denies difficulty swallowing, food or liquid getting stuck, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, constipation, diarrhea, rectal bleeding, or unintentional weight loss, though she notes a decreased appetite over the past two months due to work stress as a paralegal. Past medical history includes anxiety and seasonal allergies. Family history is notable for esophageal cancer on her maternal grandmother's side and acid reflux in her mother.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: Weight is pretty stable, but notes decreased appetite for the past two months due to work stress. Denies unintentional weight loss.
GI: Positive for acid reflux/heartburn (burning in chest and throat) worsening over the past few years. Denies dysphagia, difficulty swallowing, food getting stuck, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, or rectal bleeding.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Normal physical exam per new patient template, except for well-healed abdominal surgical scars noted, which the patient reports is from surgery as an infant (around one month old) for twisted intestines.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), poorly controlled on current omeprazole regimen. Suspect likely GERD with underlying functional etiology as well. Reassuringly, she has no unintentional weight loss and denies any dysphagia.
2. Dietary modifications: Discussed eliminating trigger foods including spicy foods, carbonated beverages, citrus, and tomato-based products.
3. Stress management: Discussed addressing high work stress and anxiety as a symptom trigger.
4. Medications: Discontinue omeprazole and switch to Nexium 40 mg twice daily; prescription to be sent to pharmacy on file. CHIEF COMPLAINT
Numbness and tingling in both hands.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 60-year-old, right-handed male referred for evaluation of bilateral hand numbness and tingling present for a few weeks, which has gotten worse over the last month. The patient reports a car wreck last December where he broke both wrists and hit his head (resulting in a head contusion), and noticed the symptoms more once they healed. He wears a wrist splint on the right (which is worse) and sometimes on the left, and the splint helps. He also reports mild stiffness in his neck. On the right side, tingling and numbness extend from the middle and ring finger up the forearm; on the left, symptoms extend from the pinky and ring finger. Symptoms are accompanied by soreness, occasional throbbing, weakness when using them, and dull tingling when pain goes away. Symptoms occur more at night and come and go throughout the day. He reports general decreased sensitivity in his hands, though he can still feel. He was given nerve pain medicine but has not been taking it as directed. Past medical history includes hypertension (taking Coreg), anxiety (taking Lexapro), and prediabetes (controlled by diet). No history of thyroid issues.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue and weight gain.
Eyes: Positive for floaters.
Cardiovascular: Positive for shortness of breath and leg swelling.
Gastrointestinal: Positive for excessive appetite and bloating.
Endocrine: Positive for always being hungry.
Skin: Positive for nail bed changes, dryness, and itching.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for gout and muscle pain.
Remainder of the review of systems is negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurologic examination:
Right hand: Sensation is normal, except pinprick sensation is diminished in the third and fourth fingers.
Left hand: Sensation is decreased in the fourth and fifth fingers.
Reflexes: 1+ and symmetric; 2+ knees; toes are downgoing bilaterally.
Tinel sign: Positive at both wrists and both elbows.
Rest of examination is normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, or potentially bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome. Symptom presentation suggests bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, as the nerves in the wrists are aggravated by past trauma.
Plan:
1. Schedule a nerve test (EMG test) to measure nerve responsiveness and pinpoint the source of nerve irritation.
2. Patient is to return for a follow-up visit after the tests are complete.
3. Consider a referral to the hand clinic (possibly for injections or carpal tunnel release surgery) or an orthopedist if symptoms persist.
4. Continue wearing wrist splints.

Constitutional is significant for impaired ability to carry out daily functions. Negative for fever or unintentional weight loss. GU is significant for urinary incontinence and wearing a diaper. Negative for genital sores, decreased or painful output. Neurological is significant for continued walking impairment and cognitive impairment. Negative for headaches, recent falls, or hallucinations. Psychiatric is negative for depression, excessive worrying, or mood swings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 124/80, heart rate 64, respirations 18, weight 174 pounds, pain 0/10.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood pressure and palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 49-year-old male with a history of hypertension starting at a young age and recent palpitations. He was recently in the emergency room in March with high blood pressure and palpitations, which he believes was a panic attack related to consuming a few cups of coffee without breakfast that day. He has not felt the palpitations since. He reports having issues with his blood pressure since he was young, with a strong family history of high blood pressure. He was recently put on a new combination medication (Benicar HCT 40-25 containing hydrochlorothiazide) by a new primary care doctor about a month ago, and is also taking amlodipine 10 mg daily. He checks his blood pressure daily every morning, and it has been running around 146 to 155 lately. He is trying to back off on his salt intake and tries to walk on the treadmill when he can. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs sound good. Abdomen is soft, non-tender to palpation. Extremities show no ankle or foot swelling.

RESULTS
Thyroid profile from March 1st, 2021. Potassium level one week ago was 4.0.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Resistant hypertension, currently on multiple medications at max dose not yet at target.
- Add spironolactone to the regimen to help drop aldosterone levels and blood pressure.
- Discussed risks of hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone, including electrolyte balance, dehydration (watch for dizziness standing up), risk of elevated potassium, and lowered sodium levels.
- Order blood tests (metabolic panel) and schedule a follow-up in two weeks to check blood pressure and electrolytes.
- Discussed rare side effect of spironolactone-induced gynecomastia (chest tenderness, swollen or enlarged breasts); instruct patient to stop medication and notify clinic if this occurs.
- Provided education on lifestyle modifications: DASH eating plan (heart.org), keeping salt under 2000 mg/day (ideally 1500 mg/day), increasing potassium, and routine treadmill exercise for 30 minutes most days.
- If blood pressure is not controlled on spironolactone, next steps may include consideration of carvedilol (with discussion of erectile dysfunction risk) or referral to a resistant hypertension clinic for evaluation of secondary causes and potential procedures such as renal denervation.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Hospital follow-up after acute on chronic CHF exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
An 82-year-old male with a history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease presents for hospital follow-up after an acute on chronic CHF exacerbation. The patient reports that he experienced ankle swelling and severe shortness of breath, requiring him to call 911. He was placed on a mask by paramedics and taken to the emergency room, where he was found to have a blood pressure of 200/90. He admits to occasional missed doses of his medications. He also admits to dietary indiscretions, specifically consuming pizza and chicken wings while watching football with friends on weekends. Since being discharged from the hospital, where he received IV diuretics and medication adjustments, he reports feeling much better, has been compliant with his diet and medications, bought a home blood pressure cuff, and has been checking his BP every other day with good results. He denies current shortness of breath, trouble moving around, sleep problems, or chest pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for chest pain, shortness of breath, and sleep problems. Positive for past ankle swelling (now improved with trace edema).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 128/72, heart rate 79, respiratory rate 26, O2 saturation 99% on room air.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Heart: 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, stable compared to prior.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Lower Extremities: Trace edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram: Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive Heart Failure: Acute on chronic exacerbation triggered by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension. 
- Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily.
- Continue strict diet modification, avoiding salty foods (pizza and chicken wings).
- Weigh daily and call if weight gain is 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Referral to a nutritionist for dietary education.

2. Hypertension: Uncontrolled during the acute event, now improved.
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order renal artery ultrasound to rule out secondary causes.

3. Stage 3 Chronic Kidney Disease:
- Order follow-up blood work/labs to ensure tolerance of the current medication regimen.

Follow-up in 3 months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
High blood pressure and concerns regarding kidney function noted on recent blood work.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Virginia is a patient referred by her new PCP due to persistently high blood pressure despite medication adjustments. The patient reports she is taking her medications as prescribed (Norvasc 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice a day; previously on lisinopril). She checks her blood pressure a few times a week using an electronic arm cuff at home and has noted readings as high as 170/90. She states she can tell when her blood pressure is high, experiencing mild headaches on those occasions. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath (even with exertion). She reports occasional lower extremity swelling if on her feet for a long time. Diet includes high-sodium foods such as pizza, wings, and subs, especially during football season. She takes NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve) occasionally for knee and back pain. Alcohol intake consists of a couple of beers during the week and 1-2 on weekends. Family history is positive for high blood pressure in both parents and kidney disease in one parent.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
- General: Feels fine most days, busy at work. Mild headaches when blood pressure is high.
- Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No shortness of breath with exertion. Mild lower extremity swelling with prolonged standing.
- Respiratory: No shortness of breath.
- Musculoskeletal: Occasional knee and back pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- Vitals: Blood pressure 169/74, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98%.
- Neck: No jugular vein distention, no carotid bruits.
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation.
- Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, 2/6 systolic ejection murmur with an extra sound heard.
- Extremities: 1+ pitting edema bilaterally.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
- Diagnosis: Uncontrolled hypertension, multifactorial etiology.
- Tests ordered: Renal artery ultrasound, morning aldosterone levels, renin levels, and a 24-hour urine collection.
- Lifestyle modifications: Decrease alcohol intake to 1-2 drinks per week. Be judicious about decreasing salt intake. Stop taking NSAIDs (Advil, Motrin, Aleve); use Tylenol for pain instead. Keep a record of home blood pressures taken at the same time every day for the next three weeks.
- Referrals: Referral to a nutritionist to discuss dietary changes and salt reduction.
- Medications: Prescribed Cardura 4 mg once a day. Continued review of current medications (Norvasc, carvedilol).
- Follow-up: Return in 3 weeks with blood pressure log. Coordination of care with patient's PCP.

Dizziness when standing up quickly and medication/health follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male who had a heart attack about six months ago with a stent placed in the left anterior descending artery. He is concerned about the number of medications he is taking, but is currently taking aspirin, Brilinta, fish oil, and Crestor (rosuvastatin). He complains of feeling really dizzy when he stands up real fast, which may be related to his metoprolol beta-blocker. He notes he has been feeling kind of down since his heart attack and lonely living with only his dog. He has diabetes, noting fasting glucose is around 130 and he believes his A1c was close to 16. He also has stage 3 chronic kidney disease (CKD) and has not seen his nephrologist in about a year, but reports he threw away all of his Motrin and Advil. 

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for dizziness when standing up quickly, feeling down/sad since heart attack, and history of diabetes and stage 3 CKD. Denies thoughts of harming himself or others. 
All other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 127/80.
Neck: No jugular venous distention or carotid bruits appreciated.
Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base.
Lower extremities: 1+ nonpitting edema (puffiness in legs).

RESULTS
Kidney function (creatinine/blood test checked for contrast dye impact) is stable and fine. Hemoglobin a1c reported by patient as close to 16.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease / Status post MI with LAD stent: Stents are permanent; continue aspirin for life and Brilinta for another six months. Refilling medications including metoprolol, Crestor 40 mg once a day, and aspirin. No stress test indicated at this time; report any chest pain or shortness of breath. Referral placed for cardiac rehab.
2. Stage 3 chronic kidney disease: Kidney function is stable. Will reach out to Dr. Miller to make an appointment for nephrology follow-up. Avoid Motrin and Advil; use Tylenol for headaches.
3. Diabetes: Order a repeat hemoglobin a1c. Place referral for dietitian for dietary education. Will talk with primary care physician about insulin regimen.
4. Depression / Adjustment difficulty: Patient reports feeling down and lonely since heart attack. Denies suicidal or homicidal ideation. Place a referral to psychiatry for talk therapy/support regarding adjustment after heart attack and mild depression.
